Maintenance Fraud

By: Tebadi Mmotla | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A broken maintenance court systems fails mothers seeking financial assistance.

Unique Selling Point:
The maintenance court operates under a broken structure and system. This makes it difficult for applicants, who majority are mothers to get the financial help they desperately need. The failure of the courts to ensure that the parents pay their dues, continues to fail the children who the courts are designed to protect.

Summary:
Single who have taken their ex-partners to different maintenance courts across South Africa accuse the courts of failure to enforce the law. There is corruption, allegedly carried out by the maintenance officers, and failure to send garnishee orders to the respondents. The women allege that they end up not getting maintenance to support their children. Some of them claim that they had to open several case files because the previous ones got lost. They say their cases get postponed to further dates. Reasons given vary from lack of courtrooms, missing file, lawyer feeling sick, being told to reopen the file with legal aid lawyers due to financial burden, etc. They say they even get harassed inside and outside of the maintenance court by the officers.

Script:


1 VO: Inside South Africa’s maintenance courts single parents who need financial
support for their children… run a gauntlet of backlogs and delays…as they gear
up to do battle with “the system” for their children's sake.


UPSOUND FROM CELL PHONE: I actually had no joy with them yesterday. They
couldn't tell me why the summons were not served. They had the address for the
employer but he could not give me a reason why.

3 VO: In Gqeberha, Lily Clake's divorce was settled over a decade ago, with a
maintenance order of R4000 a month for their daughter's care.


MAC: How would you say the journey has been?
LILY: Frustrating, very draining getting maintenance is potentially hit and miss. There’s
little communication.

4 VO: Despite the need for annual adjustments to account for inflation and rising
living costs, it’s never been increased. Last year, it just stopped altogether.

VISUALS OVER THE CELL PHONE: I went to court the 25th of April, I was thrown out
of court because the summons were not served to his employer. And then the
magistrate told me to pay R800 and go serve him myself.

5 VO: Now Lily just needs the Port Elizabeth maintenance court to directly deduct
maintenance from the defaulting parent's salary. She's requesting what’s called
an attachment order or garnishee - a service she should be able to access for
free.

VOICE OF MAINTENANCE OFFICER: Where is the guy?

LILY UNDERCOVER UPSOUND: He lives in Jeffreys Bay… I can’t afford R800 and
petrol to go serve this man.

6 VO: Getting a garnishee order from the maintenance court often takes so long
that parents opt for a private sheriff to make progress.

LILY UPSOUND THE SECOND WHATSAPP CLIP FROM 0:10: I will come back on
Monday early, and try again. But it was interesting to sit with other women all
complaining about the exact same thing.

6 VO: Single parenthood is hard enough without having to battle an unresponsive
co-parent over money for a child’s care…that’s why maintenance officers are
meant to protect children from their parents’ tug of war.

PAUSE

At one Johannesburg Magistrates Court, our producer, posing as a distressed
mother of an abusive ex, learns that she must personally take the summons.
Court officials won’t do it for her.

TEBADI: But why is it that the law forces me to go with the police and…
MO: You are not forced. You can serve it via the court if you want…but it's going to take
longer.

7 VO: In East London we meet Zandile, who asks us to hide her identity - she’s
battled since her son was little to get maintenance.

MAC: Ten years later, you're still fighting at maintenance court. Why?
ZANDILE: There are so many things. The file has gone missing a number of times. A
number of times there is no one to listen to you

UPS QUESTION FROM MAC: what are some of the reasons for him not being served
and the sheriff not even finding him?

UPS ZANDILE: I was actually giving the work address because I didn’t know where he
stayed. But each time they still said they didn’t get him at work.

8 VO: Complicating matters - the father lives in another province and Zandile
would wait months for the court - in the end paying for the service.

ZANDILE: I had to take the summons, and make sure they get where he resides. If you
leave it to the state, then you just wait... and they will tell you that there is nothing they
can do.

AYESHA: The applicants themselves shouldn’t be made to do all that work themselves.

10 VO: Cape Town Family Law expert Ayesha Karim says just because
maintenance courts are overcrowded, it doesn’t mean parents should be the ones
pressured to get the court’s work done.

AYESHA: You can go to court without legal presentation and do it yourself, likewise with
service. Of course, the sheriff charges a fee. That fee can range from a few hundred
and sometimes when it’s rural areas and it’s difficult to locate the respondent
thousands….

11 VO: When Zandile’s son was 10 years old she asked the maintenance officer
for an increase. The court basically told her she was being greedy.

ZANDILE: At that time I was asking R3000 for a 10-year-old. That magistrate blatantly
told me that R3000 was too much for a 10-year-old. When she saw the school my child
goes to, she told me, I'm taking my child to a luxury school. I'm not talking about a
private school, I am talking about a former Model C school.

12 VO: Zandile complained about the magistrate and was assigned another one.

ZANDILE: We've actually as a society accepted that, you know what, if you are the
mother, you must take care of the child. Yes I do maintain the child, but the money is
not enough. So when the father says I can’t afford this, then they say as a mother you
must see to it.

LILY: The anxiety sets in because you feel like you are failing as a mother, a supporter
of your own child.
